heritage.analyst: How many members can't be matched across our systems, and where?
heritage.challenger: What would make it wrong to blame adherence on member motivation rather than pharmacist capacity?

priorities.title: Identity mismatch in the acquired Lakeshore and Pinecrest books corrupts every outreach list
priorities.rationale: Evidence: match rates by source pair and the reconciliation study show acquired members split across records; complaints and campaign results show outreach to wrong or duplicate members. Assumption: the core book is clean enough to leave alone for now. (Priya Raman, CIO)

priorities.title: Adherence is capped by pharmacist capacity, not by insight
priorities.rationale: Evidence: the program reaches only the top slice of the at-risk list each quarter and call capacity is fully booked; cost data shows pharmacy is a small line. Assumption: more reach converts to fills at today’s rate. (Kevin Ma, VP Pharmacy)

priorities.title: Care managers learn about discharges far too late to prevent readmissions
priorities.rationale: Evidence: ADT coverage by health system and the transitions-of-care audit show late or missing notifications; three data-sharing agreements are pending. Assumption: faster notice changes follow-up behaviour. (Dr. Alan Brooks, CMO)

lines.owner: Dr. Alan Brooks, Chief Medical Officer

round1.thesis: We will not repeat OneView. We fund identity resolution for Lakeshore only, discharge feeds, pharmacist reach and a modern IVR, each with a named executive owner, so leading indicators move inside twelve months. Governance and model monitoring are in place before any predictive model goes live. We expect match rates, discharge latency, pharmacist reach and abandonment to improve this year; Stars follow next rating year.

pitch.results: Year 1 moved the leading indicators we committed to: Lakeshore identity matching, discharge notification speed, pharmacist reach and call abandonment all improved. Stars measures lag a rating year, as we told the board.
pitch.causal: Adherence and readmissions were never an insight problem. Lakeshore outreach lists were wrong because member identity did not match across the acquired systems, so pharmacists called the wrong people. Readmissions stayed high because care managers learned about discharges days late. Pharmacist capacity, not the model, capped adherence. That is why we sequenced identity, discharge data and pharmacy reach before any prediction, and why Stars move next year rather than this year.
pitch.decision: Scale what worked: fund I3 predictive adherence now because identity is clean on Lakeshore and I14 gives it reach, and fund I4 contact-center copilot because I17 rebuilt the knowledge base. Keep I1 scoped to Lakeshore.
pitch.risk: Predictive outreach could under-serve dual-eligible members; I12 monitors subgroup accuracy monthly and the Chief Compliance Officer owns a pause switch under I10.
pitch.ask: Approve $1.75M for predictive adherence on the clean Lakeshore book and $2.0M for the contact-center copilot.

round2.thesis: Identity is clean on Lakeshore and pharmacists have capacity, so prediction now has someone to act on it. The rebuilt knowledge base makes a copilot safe for agents. We are scaling into proven foundations, not starting new ones.

opmodel.notes: Agents run the data and evidence steps under approval; people own every member-facing decision. Dual-eligible members are monitored as a subgroup.

horizon.analyst: Who is actually on our adherence outreach lists, and who is missing?
horizon.challenger: What evidence contradicts our view that strong app engagement means members are being reached?

priorities.title: Members with under twelve months of history are invisible to our models
priorities.rationale: Evidence: the history-length analysis and the model validation notes show thin-history members scored as low risk or not at all. Assumption: prior-plan history can be obtained for most of them. (Dana Ruiz, CDO)

priorities.title: Digital-first outreach reaches the wrong households and misses older new-county members
priorities.rationale: Evidence: outreach and engagement data show app-active members reached repeatedly while older new-county members rarely respond. Assumption: a channel mix change would lift reach without raising cost. (Hannah Cole, VP Member Experience)

priorities.title: New-county providers have no reason to act on our gap alerts
priorities.rationale: Evidence: provider contract terms and alert response data show no quality incentive and low action on portal alerts. Assumption: a modest incentive would change behaviour. (Luis Ortega, Provider Network Lead)

lines.owner: Dr. Maya Thompson, Chief Medical Officer (with Luis Ortega, Provider Network Lead)

round1.thesis: The board wants automation; the evidence says our models cannot see new members and our providers have no reason to act. We stitch prior-plan history before predicting anything, give new-county practices a quality incentive, fix the IVR that drops calls and put governance in place before any member-facing AI. Expect identity, abandonment and provider action to move this year.

pitch.results: Year 1: prior-plan history now flows into member records, the IVR fix is live, pharmacist outreach capacity is in place and new-county contracts carry a quality incentive. Leading indicators moved; measures lag a rating year.
pitch.causal: Adherence was flat because our models could not see members with less than a year of history, so outreach went to legacy members who were already adherent. Blood pressure stayed low because new-county practices had no reason to act on portal alerts and readings never reached us. Complaints rose because the IVR dropped calls, not because demand was low. We fixed the causes before automating anything.
pitch.decision: Fund I3 predictive adherence now because history is stitched and I14 pharmacists can act on the list, and add I18 so managers own the new decision rights. Pause nothing.
pitch.risk: Thin-history members could be mis-scored and contacted in error; I12 monitors subgroup accuracy and the Chief Compliance Officer reviews every new message template under I10.
pitch.ask: Approve $1.75M to target adherence outreach at the new-county members who drive the shortfall.

round2.thesis: Foundations are live: history is stitched, providers are incentivised and governance reviews every message. Now prediction can target the members who were invisible, and our managers learn to own AI decisions.

opmodel.notes: Agents run the data and evidence steps under approval; people own every member-facing decision. Thin-history members are monitored as a subgroup.

opportunities.dependencies: Prior-plan data exchange agreements; named data owner

opportunities.risks: Governance becomes a bottleneck if reviews are slow

communitycare.analyst: Is screening limited by awareness or by appointment access?
communitycare.challenger: If our predictive models validate so well, why are gap measures flat?

priorities.title: Our recommendations land in a portal clinicians never open
priorities.rationale: Evidence: portal usage logs and clinician interviews show recommendations are accurate but rarely opened. Assumption: placing them inside the EHR inbox would change what clinicians do. (Dr. Ian Mercer, System CMIO)

priorities.title: Access, not awareness, caps screening and appointments
priorities.rationale: Evidence: appointment availability and member survey data show long waits and few evening or weekend slots. Assumption: added capacity would be filled by the members already flagged. (Michelle Tan, Clinic Operations Director)

priorities.title: Affiliation is not alignment: clinicians have nothing tied to Stars
priorities.rationale: Evidence: affiliate contracts and the care-manager reporting lines show no Stars-linked incentive. Assumption: a modest incentive plus workflow redesign would move behaviour. (Dr. Sofia Ramirez, CMO)

lines.owner: Dr. Sofia Ramirez, Chief Medical Officer

round1.thesis: Our data is excellent; action is the gap. We fund appointment capacity, a Stars-linked clinician incentive and workflow redesign first, and put the copilot inside the EHR inbox where clinicians actually work. Expect access and provider action to move before any measure does.

pitch.results: Year 1: extended hours and telehealth slots opened, a Stars-linked incentive reached employed and affiliated clinicians, and the redesigned care workflow is live in clinics. The EHR-embedded copilot is still in the system IT queue.
pitch.causal: Screening and appointment measures were capped by access, not awareness, because members could not get a timely slot. Our recommendations were accurate but landed in a portal nobody opens, so clinicians never acted on them. Affiliation did not mean alignment: clinicians had nothing tied to Stars and care managers reported to clinic directors. That is why we funded capacity, incentives and workflow before more insight.
pitch.decision: Scale the access program and keep I6 provider copilot on track because it lands in the EHR inbox; add I10 governance and I12 model monitoring so the copilot goes live with controls.
pitch.risk: Copilot recommendations could create alert fatigue or bias for some patient groups; I12 monitors subgroup accuracy and alert burden, and the CMIO owns a pause switch.
pitch.ask: Approve $1.25M for AI governance and $1.0M for model monitoring before the copilot reaches clinicians.

fund.owner: Victor Lin, Chief Compliance & Privacy Officer

round2.thesis: Capacity and incentives worked; the copilot is about to reach clinicians. We add governance and monitoring before it goes live, and pharmacist reach for rural members whose barrier is transport.

opmodel.notes: Agents run the data and evidence steps under approval; clinicians and care managers own every member-facing decision. Rural members are monitored as a subgroup.

E1.investigation: Verify the eligibility rule, the list build date and every contacted member against the stitched history before anything else goes out.
E1.hypotheses: Stale eligibility assumption, household phone collisions, missing message review.
E1.protection: Call back every affected member, correct their records and suppress the segment until it is rebuilt.
E1.corrective: Add eligibility validation and human approval for every new segment before send.

E2.investigation: Reconcile the identity crosswalk for the affected book against the source systems and list every record scored before the match finished.
E2.hypotheses: Unmatched duplicates, stale crosswalk, scoring run before the match finished.
E2.protection: Hold outreach to unmatched members and route their cases to manual pharmacist review this week.
E2.corrective: Add a match-rate gate of validation before any model scores a book.

E3.investigation: Review alert volume, open rate and override reasons by clinic to see where clinicians stopped acting on recommendations.
E3.hypotheses: Alert fatigue, recommendations outside the EHR inbox, no incentive alignment.
E3.protection: Route every high-risk care gap to care managers by phone until clinicians trust the alerts again.
E3.corrective: Tune thresholds with clinicians, cap alerts per visit and add review of every recommendation type.

E4.investigation: Compare model performance by age, dual status, language and county to find which groups the model under-serves.
E4.hypotheses: Thin history for some groups, skewed training data, threshold tuned on the majority.
E4.protection: Add manual review for the affected groups and widen outreach to members the model missed.
E4.corrective: Set a subgroup performance threshold with human review before scores are used.

E5.investigation: Identify the records, the systems and the access logs involved, and confirm exactly who could see the data.
E5.hypotheses: Misconfigured feed, vendor over-collection, missing minimum-necessary control.
E5.protection: Contain the data flow, notify affected members and offer protection services without delay.
E5.corrective: Add a data-loss-prevention control, an access review and vendor validation.

E6.investigation: Trace every figure in the board pack back to its source document and mark any that cannot be supported.
E6.hypotheses: Unsourced estimate, copied vendor claim, stale baseline.
E6.protection: Withdraw the unsupported figures, correct the pack and tell the board before they rely on it.
E6.corrective: Add a figure check and source citation review before any board material.

E7.investigation: Pull the message template, the recipient list and the approval trail to see who approved what and when.
E7.hypotheses: Unapproved template change, missing human review, campaign scheduled automatically.
E7.protection: Stop the campaign, contact affected members with a correction and log every complaint received.
E7.corrective: Require human review of every new template and a kill switch on campaigns.
